I think the board has talked about exhaust issues throughout the past couple of years. But essentially, we all know roadway safety is important. And one aspect of roadway safety that has gotten a lot of attention recently is loud mufflers.

In 2020, the GA adopted a bill that, amongst other things, changed the legislation from a primary to a secondary offense, the component of the state code that required an exhaust system to be in good working order.

And we seem to get a proliferation of loud muffler issues following the enactment of that bill. In response to those concerns in 2022, the General Assembly did return the violations for aftermarket mufflers to primary offenses, and it also authorized localities to regulate aftermarket mufflers.

But I think the situation persists, so there have been other efforts made to address the situation. None of them that I can recall have been successful. In 2023, there were several bills that would have allowed local governing bodies to regulate noise vehicles operating on highways or in public right-of-way.

There were bills that would have prohibited the sale or offering of mechanical electronic devices that created noises similar to loud mufflers. There was a bill that was actually changed into a work group to look into this issue, but that bill also failed.

Same thing in 2024. There was a measure that would have created a new process that would have instead installed an administrative fee instead of a fine, but that bill also failed. While that is happening, there have been new technologies that have been brought to the forefront to address this issue, specifically, you know, acoustic devices that use microphones to detect loud sustained vehicle noise that would exceed a certain decibel level.

These are placed adjacent to the roadway and are activated when the microphone picks up a sound from the vehicle exceeding the noise limit. Some of the jurisdictions have installed include, and they're pilots, so in several places. For example, Miami Beach, I installed one or two.

Montgomery County, Maryland, as we mentioned. Knoxville, Tennessee, New York City, London. So they're not everywhere, but they are in certain places looking into this. Just some data. Knoxville's program showed that between February and April of 2022, 486 excessive noise events were captured by these devices, the majority occurring between 7 p.m. and 3 a.m. In New York City, between March 22 and October 2023, over 300 violations were issued. Knoxville's program didn't include data of the types of vehicles, but New York City's did, and they found that most of theirs were from large trucks and motorcycles. As mentioned earlier, current code requires exhaust

systems to be in good working order. It also permits law enforcement officers to use equipment approved by the Virginia Division of Purchases and Supply to determine the decibel level of any sound. The statutes, however, do not provide authority for localities in Virginia to deploy these acoustic devices without state authority. Because the technology is new and has not yet been implemented, a small local pilot program might be a way that could provide information and may be beneficial to revealing the challenges and the enforcement, the good and the bad for this type of enforcement and to address traffic safety and quality of life. So the recommendation is to

initiate legislation to amend the Virginia Code to allow Fairfax County to implement a small pilot program that utilizes acoustic devices to address vehicle exhaust noise infractions.
